items.title: External sandboxes for coding agents
items.summary:
External sandboxes for coding agents

I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code that is executed by agents, with a focus on making it safer to try out local models without worrying that a mistake or prompt injection attack might cause them to take damaging actions on a machine.

I worked on this project with Prime Radiant, the AI research lab behind Superpowers and other projects.

My post on the Prime Radiant blog introduces the external sandbox pattern, where code executed by the agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox while the agent itself lives outside of that sandbox.

To demonstrate this pattern we've released three sandbox server implementations:

  • external-sandbox-v86 runs a Node.js server which then uses v86 to run Alpine Linux inside WebAssembly.
  • external-sandbox-container is a Python web server which runs the sandbox in Alpine Linux inside an Apple Containers instance.
  • external-sandbox-quicksand is another Python web server, this time using Microsoft's Quicksand sandboxing library, which bundles QEMU and Alpine Linux in a Python package!

Each of these implementations offers the same localhost API. You can then configure Pi, Claude Code, or Codex to send API calls to that sandbox any time they want to execute code.

The sandboxes also include an optional HTTP/HTTPS allow-list proxy, so you can control exactly which hosts your agent's code is allowed to communicate with - plus a credential replacement mechanism to make authenticated API calls without sharing a secret with the agent. Here's the UI you can use to reconfigure that proxy while the sandbox is still running:

I continue to be fascinated by the challenge of safely running untrusted code. This external sandbox pattern provides a neat way to experiment with different approaches.

Tags: sandboxing, security, ai, webassembly, generative-ai, llms, coding-agents, claude-code, codex, pi

items.title: Microsoft's agent-framework on PyPI shipped a credential stealer in two releases
items.story_key: story|title:microsoft s agent framework on pypi shipped a credential stealer in two releases
items.content_excerpt: agent-framework 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, two malicious releases of Microsoft Agent Framework's PyPI meta-package published 33 minutes apart on Nov 17, 2026, run a credential stealer on every Python start that targets Azure, Azure DevOps, and GitHub Actions secrets. Both have been removed from PyPI. Pin agent-framework==1.26.0 and rotate every secret on any machine that installed either version. You're affected if you installed agent-framework 1.26.1 or 1.26.2 between 20:35 UTC and roughly 21:20 UTC on Nov 17, 2026, whether directly or through a loose requirement like agent-framework>=1.26 . The package sees about 190,000 downloads a month, so even a 45-minute window adds up. CI is where this hurts most. A pipeline or container build that resolved a fresh install during that window ran the stealer with whatever the job had access to. On Azure DevOps that means SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN and the pipeline's service connections. On GitHub Actions, 1.26.2 goes after the OIDC token any workflow with id-token: write can request. Developer laptops and Azure VMs with a managed identity attached are exposed too. If you are an Aikido user, check your central feed and filter on malware issues. This will surface as a 100/100 critical issue. Aikido rescans nightly, but we recommend triggering a manual rescan now. If you are not yet an Aikido user, you can create an account and connect your repos. Our malware coverage is included in the free plan, no credit card required. For future protection, consider Aikido Safe Chain (open source). Safe Chain sits in your existing workflow, intercepting npm, npx, yarn, pnpm, and pnpx commands and checking packages against Aikido Intel before install. For broader coverage across your whole team, Aikido's Device Protection gives you visibility and control over the software packages installed on your team's devices. It covers browser extensions, code libraries, IDE plugins, and build dependencies, all in one place. Stop malware before it gets installed. items.title: Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review
items.story_key: story|title:harvard researchers find ai coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review
items.content_excerpt: Editor’s Note: Engineers at firms that adopted AI coding agents added about 30 percent more code, yet finished work did not measurably rise and getting code through review took 49 percent longer, according to a working paper by Harvard Ph.D. candidates Fiona Chen and James Stratton covering 718 firms. The paper, a job-market paper with no indication of completed peer review, measures what happens at the human checkpoint once drafting speeds up. Harvey’s motion-to-dismiss workflow and Cooley’s redaction agent, still in development with Google Cloud, both keep a lawyer at a comparable checkpoint, and neither announcement reports a measure of that review stage. For eDiscovery, privacy and compliance professionals, the study suggests a measurement approach for legal AI buyers: consider approved work product, revision rates and reviewer time alongside drafting output. It also shows that AI authorship can leave metadata in collaboration systems that records and legal hold programs may need to reach. Watch for a revised version of the paper and for any legal vendor that publishes review-stage figures, keeping in mind that the study examined software, not legal work. A short percentage-based assessment of the qualitative benefit expressed as a percentage of positive reception of the recent article from ComplexDiscovery OÜ titled, "Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review." Engineers at firms that adopted AI coding agents added about 30 percent more code, but finished work did not measurably rise and getting code through review took 49 percent longer, a Harvard working paper found. In the study’s data, the extra coding produced no detectable rise in finished work, and code review became the bottleneck. Fiona Chen and James Stratton, both Ph.D. candidates at Harvard University, measured that pattern across 725,938 workers at 718 companies. Chen and Stratton built the study on data from Jellyfish, a company that sells an analytics platform tracking engineering activity, and joined it to LinkedIn employment records collected by Revelio Labs. items.title: Show HN: Shard – Distributed AI Inference Across Multiple Computers
items.story_key: story|title:shard distributed ai inference across multiple computers
items.content_excerpt: Local LLM inference engine with pre-flight model fit checks, GGUF/PyTorch backends, OpenAI-compatible API, and LAN VRAM pooling (experimental P2P/WAN relay) One Network. Many Servers. Shared AI Infrastructure. Distributed local LLM inference engine pooling GPU VRAM and system RAM across LAN machines — powered by PyTorch, FastAPI, llama.cpp RPC, and native C++20 / MASM AVX2 SIMD kernels. SHARD Distributed Inference Cluster: Central master coordinator pooling VRAM across connected LAN worker nodes over UDP discovery ( :8001 ) and FastAPI SSE endpoints ( :8000 ). Overview · How It Works · Features · Quick Start · CLI Reference · Architecture · Dashboard · Community SHARD ( shard-engine ) is an open-source distributed local LLM inference engine written in Python ( FastAPI + PyTorch ) with a GGUF / llama.cpp backend and native C++20 / MASM AVX2 SIMD acceleration. Running capable 14B, 32B, or 70B+ open-weight language models locally typically hits a hard hardware wall: single-card VRAM limits . Most developers, labs, and small teams own multiple machines—a desktop gaming GPU, a workstation laptop, an auxiliary mini-PC—whose memory sits fragmented across the local network while no single device can fit the full model weights and KV cache. SHARD unites idle GPUs and system memory across your Local Area Network (LAN) into a single logical inference cluster: SHARD turns distributed local AI infrastructure into a four-step workflow: CREATE → SHARE → CONNECT → USE . Start a local SHARD node with shard start or python main.py . The engine probes your CPU, system RAM, and NVIDIA CUDA / Apple MPS GPU via hardware.py , loads your chosen GGUF or Hugging Face model, and brings up the FastAPI server and Web UI on http://localhost:8000 . Open a LAN compute pool with shard lan create --open (or generate a pairing code via shard lan create ). SHARD broadcasts UDP discovery beacons on port 8001 and exposes /api/lan/* endpoints so peer machines on your subnet can pool their VRAM and RAM. On any secondary computer on the network, run shard lan join <master-ip> --share . The worker completes an HTTP handshake ( POST /api/lan/pair ), launches its local RPC tensor worker, sends periodic health heartbeats, and contributes its GPU/RAM to the cluster. Connect coding IDEs, autonomous AI agents, or custom Python apps to http://<master-ip>:8000/v1/chat/completions or /v1/messages . items.title: How the Claude Code team thinks about verification
items.summary: How end-to-end, property and differential tests let coding agents verify their work with evidence, and what the Claude Code team does to keep its verifiers honest.
items.story_key: model:claude|title:how the claude code team thinks about verification
items.content_excerpt: How end-to-end, property and differential tests let coding agents verify their work with evidence, and what the Claude Code team does to keep its verifiers honest. On the Claude Code team, the vast majority of our code (~90%) is written and reviewed by Claude . At this scale, how we equip our agents to verify their work with evidence becomes extremely important. Verification loops are the building block that lets you delegate more work to Claude. Without them, you can really only run one or two Claudes at a time, because you have to check everything yourself. With them, you can run dozens or hundreds in parallel. That’s because giving agents a way to verify their output is an effective way to improve quality. In internal testing around structured file generation, having a separate grader check Claude’s work against a rubric improved task success by up to 10 points over a standard prompting loop, with the largest gains on the hardest problems. What was once expensive to verify (tests, benchmarks, specs, real end-to-end runs) is now cheap to request from an agent. Like code, agents can quickly generate tests, benchmarks, and specs. And once generated, these tests and benchmarks run as software so they can be run frequently without using many additional tokens. You can also close the verification loop by using the results to improve the agent’s performance on that task. For example, if an agent repeatedly fails a test that checks logs for user data, you can create a hook or a more explicit rule in your CLAUDE.md to avoid future issues. This (mostly) stops issues from happening again. So if verification is critical to producing quality code at a high velocity, what types of tests should you use and how should you apply them across your pipeline? This article answers those questions and also shares the process used by the Claude Code team. If your tests are flaky you’ll train the agent to run them again rather than fixing the failing code. If your tests are slow, the agent will do fewer tests across batches which can make pinpointing issues difficult. Heavier tests are best deployed before you’ve committed the changes. If you have to focus on one test type, pick end-to-end. These tests describe real user flows like adding an item to a cart, checking out, and moving to a confirmation page. items.title: Protect sensitive data in your traces: new controls in LangSmith
items.summary: New controls are now in LangSmith to help teams manage access to sensitive trace data. Learn more.
items.story_key: story|title:protect sensitive data in your traces new controls in langsmith
items.content_excerpt: You can’t run agents in production without governing the data they touch. When that data includes sensitive customer information, controlling access becomes a regulatory and contractual obligation. That puts engineering and security requirements at odds. Engineers need production traces to debug issues and improve agent performance. Security and compliance teams need to enforce least privilege: people should only see the data their job requires. That’s why we’ve added three new controls to LangSmith to help teams manage access to sensitive trace data: Traces give engineers visibility into how an agent behaved and help them identify what needs to improve. When they record production activity, their inputs and outputs often contain sensitive customer data, such as names, health information, or payment details. Companies need to restrict access to this data to meet: First, they can create custom observability setups with duplicate traces and multiple workspaces. Engineers get trace access, but platform teams have more to configure and maintain. The alternative is to avoid sending traces to observability platforms altogether, preventing agent engineers from having visibility and slowing product velocity. We built these new controls so organizations can meet the needs of their engineering and security teams without the messy workarounds. Here’s how it works. You send your traces to LangSmith with full data fidelity, then grant access to only those who need it. Debugging is handled with least privilege, so addressing performance issues like latency can be managed without exposing any sensitive data. If a customer reports an issue, you can grant access to only that customer’s inputs and outputs, and only to the people or teams required to address it. Everything is configurable through granular admin controls. LangSmith’s new input and output controls give admins greater control over what portions of a trace users can see. Trace inputs and outputs are where sensitive user data most often resides. Other trace data like run trees, performance stats, and metadata are critical for agent improvement and far less sensitive. With these controls, agent engineers can spot and resolve issues – like repetitive or slow tool calls – without seeing sensitive content, and those who need the full picture can be granted access as needed. items.title: claude-code v2.1.327
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added a confirmation before /install-github-app changes a repository
  • Added claude mcp add-json <name> - to read the server's JSON from stdin, so tokens can stay off the command line; not available inside a Claude Code session
  • Added a line when a resumed session's earlier messages can't be loaded
  • Added a list in /status of broken agent, skill, command and output style files, keybinding errors, an unavailable sandbox, ignored permission settings and hook matchers that never match
  • Added a note in /config when other settings override a row
  • Added x-claude-code-managed-settings-checksum to the gateway hint headers; sent where managed settings set CLAUDE_CODE_GATEWAY_HINT_HEADERS=1, including where they already do
  • Added support for naming a session's billing group with the attributionProject setting, for Claude apps gateways that set admin.billing_group_tag
  • Added /tui classic as the name for the non-fullscreen renderer; /tui default still works
  • Remote Control: Fixed stopping the server in worktree mode deleting a running session's git-ignored files, such as .env
  • Fixed self-hosted runners with --use-anthropic-git-proxy deleting a non-empty directory named by GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL at startup: the runner now keeps it, ignores the variable and warns
  • Fixed claude mcp add and claude mcp remove with project scope deleting other top-level keys from .mcp.json, such as $schema or another tool's servers
  • Fixed /export overwriting an existing file without asking: the dialog now asks, and /export <name> keeps the file and says to run /export
  • Fixed a command you had allowed still running after you pressed Stop, when the approval arrived after a restart, in cloud and self-hosted runner sessions with no feature flags loaded
  • Fixed Enter closing /teleport's load error screen
  • Fixed a click followed by Enter in /plugin installing or disabling a plugin
  • Fixed a half-typed ! command running on an extra Enter after the usage limit menu
  • Fixed some --disallowedTools rules with parentheses in their content
  • Fixed auto mode ignoring some wildcard PowerShell allow rules that name a script with .\, such as PowerShell(.\scripts\build.ps1 *)
  • Fixed a running Code Mode script in auto mode getting permission prompts and denials once Claude started a second script that auto mode also allowed
  • Changed some pre-started background sessions to be discarded after an account change
  • Changed a workflow paused at a usage limit in the terminal to stay paused after a login, until the earlier login returns or you type a prompt
  • Fixed a nested claude with its own token being refused by forceLoginOrgUUID: commands that don't get the session's token no longer get its CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_SCOPES; set it on any that need it
  • Fixed headless sessions losing stored messages on resume when a message was sent again with the same UUID after the process was killed
  • Fixed cases where a session resumed after an empty reply or a killed command lost an answer, or brought back a rewound prompt, after another crash or a move to the background
  • Fixed a remote session forgetting messages sent after Stop was pressed during a restart, if Claude Code then crashed
  • Fixed tasks created after /clear being lost, and cleared tasks coming back, when a cloud or self-hosted runner session with no feature flags loaded resumed later
  • Fixed a compaction right after a reply cut at the output token limit losing that reply's tool call and its result
  • Fixed a settings change from /config and similar commands failing to save with no warning; a line under the prompt now says so
  • Fixed /rewind closing without a word when some files could not be restored
  • Fixed pasted images being dropped when the prompt starts with a file path such as /tmp/a.txt
  • Fixed agents passed with --agents being lost once plugins loaded or reloaded
  • Fixed a plugin's agent being dropped when resuming a session from the --resume picker
  • Fixed Claude Code refusing to start when https_proxy or HTTPS_PROXY is a bare host:port and neither its input nor its output is a terminal (the desktop app, an SDK, cron)
  • Fixed Claude Code on Linux sometimes returning to the shell while restarting itself at startup, such as after the first sign-in to a Claude apps gateway or when turning on Code Mode
  • Fixed claude -p hanging before its first request when the fetch of a model's settings stalled, such as at a proxy; it now goes on without them after 10 seconds
  • Fixed the screen staying blank or frozen after a brief out-of-memory error
  • Fixed a rare display fault that could freeze the screen or end the session
  • Fixed cloud sessions breaking when a program left thousands of connections open to the session's network proxy
  • Fixed a turn hanging when a mod's $.model.complete or $.model.classify call met a usage limit: the call now gets the API's error at once; mods should handle that error
  • Fixed stalls on a compaction reply with thousands of unclosed tags and on some very long WebFetch URLs; WebFetch now refuses a URL over 2,000 characters before any permission prompt
  • Fixed a message with thousands of @ mentions stalling before Claude replies; only the first 100 mentions are now looked up as files
  • Fixed the prompt freezing after rejecting a write to a very large file; a rejected write now shows a short preview
  • Fixed a crash when a burst of keys reached the search box in /plugin
  • Fixed a false crash report and exit code when a suspended session resumes, or at exit, where a Linux security policy blocks a process from signalling itself
  • Fixed remote MCP servers staying disconnected after a longer outage such as a VPN drop: most servers on other machines reached by hostname over https are now retried in the background for about a day
  • Fixed Edit refusing with "File has not been read yet" after a compaction on unchanged files outside the project that Claude had already read in full
  • Fixed Grep repeating or skipping results when paging with head_limit and offset; content and count results are now sorted by file path
  • Fixed Read failing on Jupyter notebooks that contain an output of an unknown type
  • Fixed NotebookEdit removing the notebook file's final newline
  • Fixed the Read tool reporting 512KB instead of the real size when a file of 10 MB or more is too large to read at once
  • Fixed the Bash tool's diff of changed files not naming files that are binary, too large or too many to show
  • Fixed artifact publishes failing with "the source file changed between approval and publish" when a synced or remote-backed folder had only changed the file's timestamp
  • Fixed a new artifact that you approved being refused in a cloud scheduled task's session, in organizations that require approval of each new artifact
  • Fixed a new artifact being refused after an app built on the Agent SDK approved it, in organizations that require approval of each new artifact
  • Fixed /artifacts showing part of your list, or "No artifacts yet", when a request for more of the list failed: it now tries again, then warns if it can't load the whole list
  • Fixed in-process agent teammates on a different model from the lead compacting at the lead's context limit and on the wrong model; they now use their own limit and model, at that model's rate
  • Fixed a finished subagent resuming on the model and effort of a sibling subagent that messaged it
  • Fixed the main conversation not being told a background agent had finished when the subagent that started it ended by itself without reading the result, outside auto mode
  • Fixed Claude reporting a background agent as still running when it had waited 30 seconds or more on a permission prompt in the desktop app, on the web and in the SDK
  • Fixed Claude not being told in auto mode when a background agent's reply to a follow-up message was dropped, and reduced repeat wake-ups there from agents waiting on background commands
  • Fixed the desktop app, Claude Code on the web and VS Code showing a raw task notification as a subagent's prompt after its background task woke it
  • Fixed messages sent from another session with "later" priority joining the running turn, instead of waiting for it to end, in Remote Control and Claude Desktop sessions
  • Fixed messages to cloud and Remote Control sessions being reported as failed with a stale address after a timeout or rate limit; Claude now says when a message may have arrived
  • Fixed cloud sessions giving no error when a UserPromptSubmit hook blocks a message sent while Claude works
  • Fixed failing hooks showing nothing: SubagentStop in background agents, SessionEnd at /clear and /resume, and CwdChanged and FileChanged in fullscreen
  • Fixed a Stop hook that failed to run being shown as having reported a problem
  • Fixed focus view keeping a finished reply hidden while a Stop hook was running
  • Fixed Claude getting a long managed PostToolUse hook output twice when a mod added context to the tool call
  • Fixed /model listing the wrong models in some terminal sessions when a project's .claude/settings.json sets ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL to an LLM gateway
  • Fixed /statusline writing to ~/.claude/settings.json when CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR points to another folder
  • Fixed claudeMdExcludes patterns on Windows not matching a path whose drive letter is written in the other case
  • Fixed claude agents and claude rm refusing to remove a fully pushed session ("The worktree has unpushed commits") when its worktree has a file or folder named HEAD at the top level
  • Fixed long ListAgents results hiding most sessions on accounts with many cloud or Remote Control sessions: long lists now come in pages
  • Fixed slow turns in resumed sessions for organizations with tens of thousands of connector tool permissions
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed claude -p started by a session's script or hook waiting out rate limits, because it inherited the session's own retry setting
  • Fixed the spend limit menu reporting a changed limit when the server refused it
  • Fixed a second x on a task's details in /tasks stopping the next task too
  • Fixed Esc being ignored on a permission prompt that had just appeared
  • Fixed lists that load their rows late sometimes ignoring Enter and the arrow keys
  • Fixed /autofix-pr holding the keyboard after Esc while it stopped the cloud session; the dialog now closes at once, and a stop that fails is reported afterwards with a link
  • Fixed a blank screen and stray mouse codes in the shell after quitting with ctrl+c just after ← opens the agents view
  • Fixed Ctrl+C right after the trust question leaving the terminal in fullscreen
  • Fixed the shell flashing on screen when ← opens the agents view in fullscreen mode
  • Fixed terminal display faults: most scrambled scrollback in Ghostty on resize, link addresses hidden in Windows Terminal under old tmux and in VTE 0.50.0, and no selection highlight with 16 colors
  • Fixed some garbled rows in tmux with allow-passthrough on inside kitty, Ghostty or iTerm2
  • Fixed /mcp saying no servers were configured after one was added during a session or declined; it now says what to do
  • Fixed /hooks leaving out hooks given by --settings
  • Fixed the / menu listing a row for each skill of the same name, though every row ran the first
  • Fixed /teleport showing no message when the chosen session failed to resume
  • Fixed n and N in transcript search skipping matches
  • Fixed cancelling a transcript search (ctrl+o, then /) in a long session landing far from where the search started
  • Fixed up and down losing the cursor's column over a short or blank line
  • Fixed Tab in shell mode filling in a file name after &&, ; or |, where a command goes
  • Fixed the selected session leaving the screen in claude --resume and /resume when branch names or folder paths are long
  • Fixed the MCP tool list in /mcp and /plugin losing your place when going back from a tool
  • Fixed /resume listing one session fewer than the window has room for, and a 'Resend your message' hint after most spend caps, where resending can't help
  • Fixed an MCP server's long question being cut off after one row, text fields hiding long pastes with no sign, and a doubled divider line in /plugin's options and /login's Bedrock and Vertex steps
  • Fixed the "+N lines" count being too high for command output with links or colors, and the transcript's ? help hiding how to exit in a short window
  • Fixed Ctrl+C twice not closing /chrome from its browser list
  • Fixed a number and Enter typed too early at an agent's plan approval in screen reader mode causing the next number to be dropped too
  • Fixed Claude trying to read design system token files that do not exist when starting a deck or design
  • Fixed exit not saying that a worktree was kept
  • Fixed /hooks help naming input fields that do not exist
  • Fixed question dialogs naming ctrl+g after the external editor key was rebound
  • Fixed two sign-in error messages that pointed to the Claude subscription option on computers where forceLoginMethod is set to console
  • Fixed /config saying the dialog was dismissed instead of "Set theme to …" after changing the theme
  • Bug fixes and reliability improvements
  • Improved the speed of a session's first Bash command: shell start-up files may now run before it's approved, even if it's refused; set CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_SHELL_HEAD_START=1 to turn this off
  • Improved commits on newer models and in PowerShell: Claude is now told not to commit files that likely contain secrets

items.title: Release 2.75.0 corresponding to NGC container 26.11
items.summary:
Triton Inference Server

The Triton Inference Server provides a cloud inferencing solution optimized for both CPUs and GPUs. The server provides an inference service via an HTTP or GRPC endpoint, allowing remote clients to request inferencing for any model being managed by the server. For edge deployments, Triton Server is also available as a shared library with an API that allows the full functionality of the server to be included directly in an application.

New Features and Improvements

  • PyTorch backend: Added AOTI BF16 input/output support.
  • THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt is now included in the containers.
  • Fixed a use-after-free in the dynamic batcher and a preserve_ordering completion-slot issue on response-cache hits.
  • Prevented silent gRPC stream cancellations under backpressure.
  • Bounded the decompressed HTTP inference response size in the client library.
  • Perf Analyzer: Honored supplied output shapes, propagated the binary exit code, tagged the wheel as platform-specific, and limited profile-data export to the needed inputs and outputs.
  • Python backend: Now logs when the backend stub exits on a crash signal.

Known Issues

  • The Triton TensorRT-LLM Backend container image is not included in this release.
  • vLLM's v0 API and Ray are affected by vulnerabilities. Users should consider their own architecture and mitigation steps which may include but should not be limited to:
    • Do not expose Ray executors and vLLM hosts to a network where any untrusted connections might reach the host.
    • Ensure that only the other vLLM hosts are able to connect to the TCP port used for the XPUB socket. Note that the port used is random.
  • When using Valgrind or other leak detection tools on AGX-Thor or DGX-Spark systems, you might see memory leaks attributed to NvRmGpuLibOpen.
  • Valgrind or other memory leak detection tools may occasionally report leaks related to DCGM. These reports are intermittent and often disappear on retry.
  • CuPy has issues with the CUDA 13 Device API in multithreaded contexts. Avoid using tritonclient cuda_shared_memory APIs in multithreaded environments until fixed by CuPy.
  • TensorRT calibration cache may require size adjustment in some cases, which was observed for the IGX platform.
  • The core Python binding may incur an additional D2H and H2D copy if the backend and frontend both specify device memory to be used for response tensors.
  • A segmentation fault related to DCGM and NSCQ may be encountered during server shutdown on NVSwitch systems. A possible workaround for this issue is to disable the collection of GPU metrics tritonserver --allow-gpu-metrics false ....
  • When using TensorRT models, if auto-complete configuration is disabled and is_non_linear_format_io:true for reformat-free tensors is not provided in the model configuration, the model may not load successfully.
  • When using Python models in decoupled mode, users need to ensure that the ResponseSender goes out of scope or is properly cleaned up before unloading the model to guarantee that the unloading process executes correctly.
  • Triton Inference Server with vLLM backend currently does not support running vLLM models with tensor parallelism sizes greater than 1 and the default "distributed_executor_backend" setting when using explicit model control mode. In attempt to load a vllm model (tp > 1) in explicit mode, users could potentially see failure at initialize step: could not acquire lock for <_io.BufferedWriter name='<stdout>'> at interpreter shutdown, possibly due to daemon threads. For the default model control mode, after server shutdown, vllm related sub-processes are not killed. Related vllm issue: vllm-project/vllm#6766. Please specify "distributed_executor_backend":"ray" in the model.json when deploying vllm models with tensor parallelism > 1.
  • When loading models with file override, multiple model configuration files are not supported. Users must provide the model configuration by setting parameter "config" : "<JSON>" instead of custom configuration file in the following format: "file:configs/<model-config-name>.pbtxt" : "<base64-encoded-file-content>".
  • TensorRT-LLM backend provides limited support of Triton extensions and features.
  • The TensorRT-LLM backend may core dump on server shutdown. This impacts server teardown only and will not impact inferencing.
  • The Java CAPI is known to have intermittent segfaults.
  • Some systems which implement malloc() may not release memory back to the operating system right away causing a false memory leak. This can be mitigated by using a different malloc implementation. Tcmalloc and jemalloc are installed in the Triton container and can be used by specifying the library in LD_PRELOAD. NVIDIA recommends experimenting with both tcmalloc and jemalloc to determine which one works better for your use case.
  • Auto-complete may cause an increase in server start time. To avoid a start time increase, users can provide the full model configuration and launch the server with --disable-auto-complete-config.
  • Auto-complete does not support PyTorch models due to lack of metadata in the model. It can only verify that the number of inputs and the input names matches what is specified in the model configuration. There is no model metadata about the number of outputs and datatypes. Related PyTorch bug: pytorch/pytorch#38273
  • Triton Client PIP wheels for ARM SBSA are not available from PyPI and pip will install an incorrect Jetson version of Triton Client library for Arm SBSA. The correct client wheel file can be pulled directly from the Arm SBSA SDK image and manually installed.
  • Traced models in PyTorch seem to create overflows when int8 tensor values are transformed to int32 on the GPU. Refer to pytorch/pytorch#66930 for more information.
  • Triton cannot retrieve GPU metrics with MIG-enabled GPU devices.
  • Triton metrics might not work if the host machine is running a separate DCGM agent on bare-metal or in a container.

Client Libraries and Examples

The client libraries and examples are available in this release exclusively via the Ubuntu 24.04–based NGC Container. The SDK container includes the client libraries and examples, Performance Analyzer, and Model Analyzer. See Getting the Client Libraries for more information.

ManyLinux Assets (early access)

This release was compiled with AlmaLinux 8.9 based out of manylinux_2_34 and can be used on RHEL 9 and later versions.
See the included README.md for complete details about installation, verification, and support.
This release supports ensembles. Confirm CUDA, TensorRT, ONNX Runtime, PyTorch, and Python versions in the shipped README.md.
Some optional backend features such as the PyTorch backend's TorchTRT extension are not currently supported.

items.title: What We’ve Learned Building Proactive Agents
items.summary: Proactive agents work toward goals in the background and check in when they need you. What we've learned about memory and UX from building GTM Agent and Robin.
items.story_key: story|title:what we ve learned building proactive agents
items.content_excerpt: Think about how you work with a new hire. In their first week, you give them small, well-scoped tasks, like triaging a bug report or updating a doc. Soon you're giving them bigger tasks, and eventually you're handing them a lofty goal and letting them figure out how to tackle it. They still come to you with clarifying questions or review requests, just less often over time. Agents have gotten good enough that you can onboard them the same way, and like a good new hire, they're turning into proactive problem solvers. Personal agents like Muse, Instinct, and OpenAI's dots popularized proactive agents, which run in the background and work toward larger goals instead of waiting for a prompt. Hone puts it most directly, describing its Engines as AI that is "assigned goals rather than tasks." Goals let these agents take on harder problems that play out over days or weeks. A proactive agent still checks in with you when it's unsure what you want or needs your sign-off before something goes out. When your direct reports get really good at their jobs, you might find that you've become the bottleneck, and the same is true for agents. As they take on more goals, your attention becomes the scarce resource. We think two things are essential to building proactive agents that use it well: memory and UX. A proactive agent responds to events in its environment, which come from three places: The examples throughout come from two proactive agents we run internally at LangChain: These agents operate on all three types of triggers. A few examples: Robin's reviews start from a real-world event, a newly opened pull request, and GTM Agent's daily brief runs on a schedule it created itself after a user requests one. We built both agents on Managed Deep Agents , where more than 70% of runs now come from schedules rather than an ad hoc human prompt. A proactive agent decides for itself when to come to you, and each check-in costs you some attention. It has to be proactive without being annoying . For an executive assistant agent that watches your inbox, that means flagging the message from your boss about tomorrow's launch without also flagging every newsletter. The agent can only tell the two apart if it knows what matters to you, and that knowledge comes from memory . Memory is the information an agent learns over time. When a proactive agent wakes up from a schedule or an event, there's no prompt from you saying what you want. It can pull in fresh context through its connectors,

items.story_key: story|title:advancing catalog interoperability with unity catalog and google cloud s borderl
items.content_excerpt: Learn how Databricks and Google are advancing interoperability through open standards. The Lakehouse architecture is becoming more open than ever. What started with open table formats – Delta Lake and Iceberg – has evolved into catalog federation for zero-copy access across multiple platforms. Through our partnership and Open Source contributions, Databricks and Google Cloud continue to drive advancements in the Open Lakehouse community. Today, we're proud to announce a significant milestone in catalog interoperability in collaboration with Google: customers can now access a single copy of data from both Unity Catalog and Google Cloud's borderless Lakehouse . The Databricks and Google Cloud partnership continues to thrive, and we're committed to making bi-directional interoperability seamless. Bringing data from Google Cloud into Databricks is simple. With Lakehouse Federation to Google Cloud , now generally available, customers can mount Iceberg tables managed by Google Cloud's Lakehouse runtime catalog in Unity Catalog for analysis in Databricks. These Iceberg tables from Google's Lakehouse runtime catalog can then be queried by Databricks Lakehouse , our serverless data warehouse, or analyzed via Genie , which intelligently answers data questions from natural language – no code or SQL required. Interoperability works in the other direction as well. Data from Databricks can also be brought into Google Cloud's Lakehouse ( learn more ). This allows customers using engines like BigQuery to read Unity Catalog managed tables without data copy. Databricks and Google Cloud are taking major strides to strengthen interoperability by making catalog metadata open. Our belief is that business and governance semantics should be accessible rather than tied to a specific vendor. In the Iceberg community, we helped drive and land catalog labels - a proposal that enables catalogs to share metadata through key-value pairs (a.k.a labels). That way, a table tagged as "domain=finance" and "status=certified" with a column tagged as "pii=ssn" continues to be tagged even as the table is federated from one catalog to another ( learn more ). Shared labels are critical for governance in the era of agents as catalog metadata can be used to flag sensitive data for masking and provide context to agents searching for assets to answer data questions. items.title: Embedding Cosine Measures Text Length Before It Measures Homogenization
items.summary: Mean pairwise cosine similarity between transformer embeddings is a standard measure of whether online discourse is converging under generative AI. When the embeddings are mean-pooled outputs of an encoder never trained for sentence similarity, this measure mostly tracks text length. In 6.06 million Reddit comments, an uncentered DeBERTa-v3 measure had suggested that only conservative discourse broke toward homogeneity after late 2022. Truncating the same comments from 10 to 150 words raises their mean cosine by eight times the reported break. A placebo that swaps every comment for a random one of equal length reproduces 81% of the asymmetry, and a fixed-content simulation reproduces 78%. The leading principal direction carries 99.9% of raw DeBERTa homogeneity, and once length is handled the asymmetry disappears under every encoder. On 575,000 Stack Exchange answers the measure reports a post-ChatGPT homogenization of technical sites that the placebo fully reproduces, although answers grew longer. A census of 31 studies locates the risk where anisotropic encoders meet time-series or length-unequal designs. A reverse control on a well-known experiment shows that centering with renormalization can reverse a genuine effect. I propose a low-cost diagnostic protocol. Corrected measures show that the two political camps converged between 2019 and 2022 and stopped converging before ChatGPT. Cross-camp replies engage their targets more closely than same-camp replies.

items.title: Latent Lattice Language Models
items.summary: Language models typically increase per-token computation through deeper or looped layers and latent reasoning steps, while richer residual connections improve information flow across layers. We instead increase computational capacity: the number of active computational states a model maintains. We introduce the Lattice of Latents, a set of per-layer horizontal latent streams that run recurrently along time, alongside the vertical residual stream that flows through depth. Like hyper-connections, mHC, and attention or value residuals, the Lattice enhances the residual stream, but rather than adding or rerouting residual pathways through depth, it provides companion computational states that persist across tokens. Unlike hybrid Transformer-SSM architectures, whose recurrent states primarily serve as internal memory for sequence mixing, these latents directly condition the vertical stream's attention, KV-cache writes, MLP computation, and decoding. On Transformers trained on 20B FineWeb-Edu tokens, a 406M-parameter Lattice model lowers validation perplexity from 15.41 to 14.40 over a parameter-matched Transformer. These gains extend across architectural variants. The Lattice composes with prior residual-stream enhancements: with hyper-connections and input residuals, it lowers validation perplexity from 15.41 (base Transformer) and 14.22 (Transformer with the same enhancements) to 13.61. On Gated DeltaNet, Mamba-2, Triadic GDN, and GDN-Mamba-2 hybrids, it improves perplexity at every tested native state size, with Lattice-GDN and Lattice-Triadic-GDN variants outperforming pure baselines with 4x larger native states. These results identify persistent per-layer state as a complementary axis for scaling language-model computation.

items.title: Algorithm Distillation for Safe In-Context Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: Safe in-context reinforcement learning (Safe ICRL) asks a policy with fixed parameters to improve on an unseen constrained task from its interaction history while aiming to keep its cost within a budget. Prior work studied Safe ICRL on five benchmarks in three families: a grid world with a hidden goal and obstacles (DarkRoom), continuous navigation where goals and hazards stay invisible until reached (PointGoal, CarGoal), and locomotion with a hidden velocity limit (HalfCheetah, Ant). Safe Algorithm Distillation (Safe AD), trained on the learning histories of a safe RL algorithm, has shown adaptation failures in prior evaluations. For example, in the locomotion tasks its return stays below zero, and it rarely reaches the goal in CarGoal. We revisit two parts of Safe AD. First, we distill a budget-aware teacher with two phases. It searches for the hidden task, exploring more when more budget remains. After its first reward or cost, an expert policy exploits the task within the remaining budget. We collect the teacher's histories under fixed or dynamic budgets. Dynamic budgets increase the occupancy entropy of the return and budget inputs in every environment, and at test time they improve return and lower cost in DarkRoom and HalfCheetah. Second, we propose A-Lag, a test-time adjustment that reweights the distilled policy's actions by their predicted cost, with an adaptive Lagrange multiplier that is updated from the costs observed. In our experiments, A-Lag had lower mean episode cost than Safe AD in all five environments, with lower mean final return in four.

items.title: H3-Image Day-0 Support: 4K in 0.87s with Vera Rubin
items.summary: H3-Image on Vera Rubin: 0.87-second 4K generation or 6,115 images/hour on four GPUs, with projected API revenue and support across consumer and data-center hardware.
items.story_key: story|variant:image|title:h3 image day 0 support 4k in 0 87s with vera rubin
items.content_excerpt: We brought MiniMax H3-Image to NVIDIA Vera Rubin with vLLM-Omni. On four GPUs, native 4096×4096 generation reaches 0.87 seconds median in our short-prompt serving benchmark. A separate throughput configuration delivers 6,115 images/hour , projecting to 146,755 images/day . At USD 0.06879 per image , using MiniMax's official Standard 4K API pricing example before launch discounts as an assumed sale price, peak throughput projects to USD 105.16/GPU/hour in gross revenue at full billable utilization, or USD 78.87/GPU/hour at 75%. These estimates are before operating costs; the daily capacity is an extrapolation of the measured rate. H3-Image is an open-weight model for text-to-image generation and image editing. One checkpoint handles both tasks in six sampling steps, generates native high-resolution images without an upscaler, and supports up to 16 reference images. We bring H3-Image to consumer and data-center GPUs , spanning NVIDIA, AMD, Intel and Moore Threads (MUSA) , as well as Huawei Ascend NPUs . Oil-paint strokes, a multi-view camera drawing, Japanese poster lettering and tiny words on a rice grain reveal what a smaller image can lose. A game environment adds weathered stone and reflected light. Each uses one H3-Image-generated 4K image, resized to 1K and 2K with its aspect ratio preserved, so composition stays fixed. The two API modes are straightforward: Text-to-Image takes a prompt; Image Edit takes a prompt and one or more reference images. Our main comparisons use 2K (2048×2048) and 4K (4096×4096) output, with one image returned per request. The prompts and reference files stay fixed across machines. See MiniMax's API guide for the request parameters. Choose Text-to-image or Image Edit below. For editing, select 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16 reference images ; output sizes reflect the measured cases. For 4K text-to-image , four GB300 GPUs average 1.48 seconds . A 4K image edit with one reference averages 1.77 seconds . A single RTX 5090 with CPU layerwise offload takes 52.29 seconds and 61.45 seconds for those same requests. Each timing includes the complete PNG response. For 2K text-to-image , a single H200 averages 1.49 seconds with BF16 and resident weights. For the detailed coffee-product prompt used here, Rubin averages 1.09 seconds at 4K. The 0.87-second headline comes from a separate short-prompt serving benchmark in Rubin Bringup , not this request.
